summary.text:
Lecture 1 is the course contract plus a highlight reel. Bloom's pitch: a state-of-the-art introduction to "the most important topic that there is: us" [1] — a sweep through brains, children, language, sex, memory, madness, disgust, racism and love [2]. The field is mapped into five sub-areas: neuroscience, developmental, cognitive, social and clinical [3].

The mechanics matter and are all on the tape: two lectures a week plus readings, and neither substitutes for the other [4]; a midterm, plus a final held on the last day of class rather than in exam period [5]; weekly pass/fail questions due to your teaching fellow [6]; and a book review plus an experimental-participation requirement [7].

The teaser topics run from Phineas Gage — the pipe through the head that left him alive but without his sense of right and wrong [8] — to Capgras syndrome, the delusion that the people you love most have been replaced [9]. The method behind the morbid catalogue: extreme cases throw normal life into sharp contrast [10].

concepts.definition: The one sub-area Bloom flags as unfamiliar: a computational approach that studies the mind on analogy with a computer — language, object recognition, game-playing.

cite.quote: it refers to a sort of computational approach to studying the mind, often viewing the mind on analogy with a computer

concepts.definition: The nineteenth-century construction worker who survived a pipe through the head but lost his self-control — the course's standing example of the brain giving rise to the mind.

cite.quote: a metal pipe went through his head like so. Miraculously, he was not killed.

concepts.definition: A delusion, typically after a stroke, that one's closest people have been replaced by impostors — evidence that recognizing something and knowing what it is are separate brain functions.

cite.quote: And the delusion is that the people you love the most have been replaced.

concepts.definition: The stranger sibling of Capgras, involving the same brain regions: the fixed belief that you are dead.

cite.quote: And Cotard's syndrome is you believe that you're dead.

concepts.term: "The child is father to the man"
concepts.definition: Wordsworth's line, used to pose the continuity question: how much of the adult — personality, interests, intelligence — is visible in the five-year-old?

cite.quote: "The child is father to the man."
